classification.difficultyReason: Connect increasing edge counts and decreasing edge lengths to a repeated perimeter multiplier, generalise using indices, and interpret unbounded growth. Successive subparts scaffold the generalisation, and calculator trial and error is explicitly supplied for the unit-converted thresholds.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Consider the equilateral triangle shown opposite. If each side of the triangle is of length 3 cm, what is the perimeter of the triangle?

spec.description: Upright equilateral triangle; one equality tick on every side. Source blue outlines are ordinary geometry and are rendered black.
spec.mathematics: Three equal sides; no numerical labels in the figure.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry is supplied; no answer is shown.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Suppose that the following procedure is performed on the triangle above: ‘On the outside of each side of the triangle, draw a triangle with side lengths one-third of the side lengths of the original triangle’.

After this procedure is done, the star shape opposite is obtained.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 2b, right-hand figure below the original triangle
spec.description: First snowflake boundary with twelve equally marked edges, an upward point and a downward point. Shared middle-third segments are absent. Ordinary source blue outlines are rendered black.
spec.mathematics: Each original side is replaced by four equal boundary segments, each one-third of its length.
spec.answerVisibility: The first-stage figure is supplied; lengths and perimeter remain unanswered.

children.label: i
children.prompt: What is the length of each edge?

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the perimeter of the star?

answer.worked: The supplied star has 12 equal edges, so $P=12\times1=12\text{ cm}$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: What is the ratio of the perimeter of this star to the original perimeter?

answer.worked: $12:9=4:3$. The new perimeter is $\frac43$ times the original perimeter.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Suppose that the procedure of part b is performed on this star (that is, each of the 12 sides has a triangle with side lengths one third of the previous ones drawn on it).

children.label: i
children.prompt: How many sides will the new star have?

answer.worked: Each of the 12 edges becomes four edges: $12\times4=48$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the length of each edge of the new star?

answer.worked: Each new edge has length $1\div3=\frac13\text{ cm}$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: What is the perimeter of the new star?

children.label: iv
children.prompt: If the perimeter of the new star can be written in the form $a^2\times9$, find the value of $a$.

answer.worked:
Each iteration multiplies the perimeter by $\frac43$.

$P=\left(\frac43\right)^2\times9$, so the positive perimeter multiplier is $a=\frac43$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Suppose that the procedure is repeated indefinitely. What will the perimeter of the shape be after the procedure has been performed:

children.label: i
children.prompt: 3 times (expressing your answer in the form $a^3\times9$)?

answer.worked:
The initial perimeter is 9 cm and each iteration multiplies it by $\frac43$:

$P_3=\left(\frac43\right)^3\times9\text{ cm}$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: 4 times (expressing your answer in a similar way)?

answer.short:
$\left(\frac43\right)^n\times9\text{ cm}$

Each iteration multiplies the perimeter by $\frac43$.
answer.worked:
There are $3\times4^n$ edges, each of length $\frac{3}{3^n}$ cm.

$$\begin{align*}P_n&=(3\times4^n)\times\frac{3}{3^n}\\P_n&=9\left(\frac43\right)^n\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Using your calculator, find, by trial and error, the number of times this procedure has to be done to produce a perimeter of at least:

answer.worked:
$1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}$.

$P_8=9\left(\frac43\right)^8<100$ and $P_9=9\left(\frac43\right)^9>100$.

The perimeter increases at every iteration, so 9 is the minimum.

$10\text{ m}=1000\text{ cm}$.

$P_{16}=9\left(\frac43\right)^{16}<1000$ and $P_{17}=9\left(\frac43\right)^{17}>1000$.

The perimeter increases at every iteration, so 17 is the minimum.

$1\text{ km}=100000\text{ cm}$.

$P_{32}=9\left(\frac43\right)^{32}<100000$ and $P_{33}=9\left(\frac43\right)^{33}>100000$.

The perimeter increases at every iteration, so 33 is the minimum.

inlines.text: If this procedure is performed indefinitely, what do you think happens to the perimeter? Does this surprise you?

The shape produced by indefinitely repeating this procedure is called the Snowflake curve. You might like to try to draw what the snowflake looks like after each of the first few applications of the procedure.

answer.short: The perimeter grows without bound. Personal responses about surprise will vary.
answer.worked: Each iteration multiplies the perimeter by $\frac43>1$, so $9\left(\frac43\right)^n$ grows without bound as the number of iterations increases. Although the individual edges become shorter, their increasing number makes the total perimeter grow. Personal responses about surprise will vary.
